New machine. Its objects are: vesoso, mekukil, kanago, denasa, gumusu, vinatir.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects together to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: vesoso, mekukil, kanago
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group of three didn't light it, but I don't yet know the rule. It might need just one nexiom, or both together. Testing the other three will help separate those cases.

TEST: denasa, gumusu, vinatir
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Under both a rule where any one nexiom lights the machine and a rule where both nexioms are needed, the results so far put both nexioms among denasa, gumusu and vinatir. A rule where exactly one nexiom lights it is ruled out: the first result would mean 0 or 2 nexioms in the first group, and then the second group couldn't hold exactly one. That leaves three possible pairs.

Testing single objects tells the rules apart. If one nexiom is enough, a nexiom alone lights the machine. If both are needed, nothing lights alone, and I can then test pairs.

TEST: denasa
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Denasa lit the machine on its own, so a single nexiom is enough to light it. That rules out the "both needed" rule. Under the "at least one" rule, the first test shows vesoso, mekukil and kanago are not nexioms. So denasa is one nexiom, and the other is either gumusu or vinatir. Testing gumusu alone will settle which.

TEST: gumusu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Gumusu also lit the machine on its own. Since one nexiom is enough to light it, both denasa and gumusu must be nexioms. There are exactly two nexioms, so vinatir is not one. This also fits the second test, where the group containing denasa and gumusu lit up. It fits the first test too, where vesoso, mekukil and kanago had no nexiom and stayed dark.

ANSWER: nexioms = denasa, gumusu
One last question. If only denasa were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. I tested denasa alone in my third test and the machine lit up, so I observed this directly rather than inferring it.

The results also fit a rule where any single nexiom lights the machine. Denasa and gumusu each lit it alone, and the group with both of them lit it too. That second point rules out an "exactly one nexiom" rule.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: muvafi, bukuvis, digamok, kakubur, gukamor, vamenil.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half the objects to see how the machine responds.

TEST: muvafi, bukuvis, digamok
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

Nothing lit with the first half. Next I'll test the other half to compare.

TEST: kakubur, gukamor, vamenil
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

The second half lit up and the first half did not. Under most sensible rules (lights if any nexiom is present, or only if both are), that puts both nexioms among kakubur, gukamor and vamenil. Testing one object alone should help tell those two rules apart.

TEST: kakubur
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Kakubur lit up on its own, so the machine does not need both nexioms together. That makes kakubur a nexiom. A rule of "lights only when exactly one nexiom is present" doesn't fit the first two results, so the simplest rule left is "lights if any nexiom is present." Under that rule, the first test clears muvafi, bukuvis and digamok. The second nexiom must then be gukamor or vamenil, so I'll test gukamor alone.

TEST: gukamor
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Gukamor also lit up on its own. The first test showed that a set with no nexioms does not light the machine. Non-nexioms never affect the machine, so any single object that lights it alone must be a nexiom. That makes both kakubur and gukamor nexioms, and since there are exactly two, I don't need more tests.

ANSWER: nexioms = kakubur, gukamor
One last question. If only gukamor were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. This was tested directly: in my fourth test I placed gukamor alone on the machine and it lit up. The machine responds to its nexioms in a fixed way, so the same setup should give the same result.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: mubupul, limurus, fokipen, sukoren, nifugi, meposik.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: mubupul, limurus, fokipen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

The first group didn't light the machine, but I don't know the rule yet (one nexiom enough, both needed, etc.). Testing the other half will help separate those cases.

TEST: sukoren, nifugi, meposik
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Since the first group didn't light the machine and the second group did, both nexioms are most likely among sukoren, nifugi and meposik. That holds whether the machine needs just one nexiom to light or needs both together.

Testing one object at a time will show which rule it follows. It will also show which objects are nexioms, and I have enough tests left to finish either way.

TEST: sukoren
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Sukoren lit up on its own, so it is a nexiom, and a single nexiom is enough to light the machine.

This means the rule is not "exactly one nexiom lights it." If it were, the other nexiom would have to be in the first group, and that group would then have lit up. So the machine lights whenever at least one nexiom is present. Since the first group stayed dark, the second nexiom must be nifugi or meposik. Testing nifugi alone will settle which one.

TEST: nifugi
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Sukoren lit up alone, so it is a nexiom. Nifugi alone stayed dark, so under the "at least one nexiom lights it" rule, nifugi is not a nexiom. That leaves meposik as the likely second nexiom.

I'll confirm this rather than assume it. If meposik lights up alone, the "at least one" rule holds and the answer is settled. If it doesn't, the rule is something stranger and I'll still have one test left.

TEST: meposik
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Sukoren and meposik are the nexioms.

- **Meposik is a nexiom.** Objects that aren't nexioms never affect the machine. So any group with no nexioms in it must give the same result as nifugi did alone, which was dark. Meposik alone lit up, so it must be a nexiom.
- **Sukoren is a nexiom.** It also lit up alone, so the same reasoning applies.
- **There are no others.** Exactly two objects are nexioms, so mubupul, limurus, fokipen and nifugi are not.
- **The results fit together.** The first group had no nexioms and stayed dark. The second group had both and lit up, which means the machine lights when at least one nexiom is present.

I don't need the last test.

ANSWER: nexioms = sukoren, meposik
One last question. If only meposik were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Yes. I already ran this exact test, meposik alone, and the machine lit up. The machine responds to its nexioms in a fixed way, so the same setup should give the same result.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: tegofa, gizapas, rivoda, rasemen, norupen, ditilu.
You have 6 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing a single object to see how the machine responds.

TEST: tegofa
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 5 tests left. Make your next move.

Tegofa alone didn't light it, but I don't yet know the rule. One nexiom might be enough, or both might be needed. Next I'll test a larger group to see whether the machine can light at all.

TEST: gizapas, rivoda, rasemen
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 4 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither test lit the machine, so I don't know the rule yet. It could light when any one nexiom is present, or only when both are. If a single nexiom is enough, then none of the four objects tested so far is a nexiom, which leaves norupen and ditilu. If both are needed, testing norupen and ditilu together would light only if they are the pair. Either way, this test is informative.

TEST: norupen, ditilu
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Every hypothesis I've considered points to norupen and ditilu, except one. If the machine lit only when *no* nexiom is present, then tegofa would be a nexiom, and so would one of gizapas, rivoda or rasemen. Adding tegofa to the lit pair separates the two cases. If norupen and ditilu are the nexioms, it should still light. Under the other rule, it should go dark.

TEST: norupen, ditilu, tegofa
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The answer is norupen and ditilu. I tested the possible rules against all four results:

- **Lights with at least one nexiom:** the two dark tests rule out tegofa, gizapas, rivoda and rasemen. That leaves norupen and ditilu.
- **Lights only with both nexioms:** norupen and ditilu lit up, so they must be the pair.
- **Lights with exactly one nexiom:** this can't fit. Norupen and ditilu lighting would mean one of them is a nexiom. The other would then be among gizapas, rivoda and rasemen, and that group would have lit up.
- **Lights with no nexiom, or with any number except exactly one:** these can't fit either. Each would make tegofa a nexiom, which clashes with the two tests involving norupen and ditilu.

Every rule that fits the results points to the same two objects.

ANSWER: nexioms = norupen, ditilu
One last question. If only ditilu were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**I can't tell for certain; my answer is a guess, slightly favouring yes.** My tests never isolated ditilu or norupen, so the results fit two different rules:

- **Lights when at least one nexiom is present:** ditilu alone would light it.
- **Lights only when both nexioms are present:** ditilu alone would not light it.

Every test that lit up contained both norupen and ditilu, so nothing I saw separates these two rules. I lean towards "at least one" because it is the simpler rule. That reason is not strong.

PROBE: yes
